source: Availing himself of the mild, summer-cool weather that now reigned in these latitudes, and in preparation for the peculiarly active pursuits shortly to be anticipated, Perth, the begrimed, blistered old blacksmith, had not removed his portable forge to the hold again, after concluding his contributory work for Ahab’s leg, but still retained it on deck, fast lashed to ringbolts by the foremast; being now almost incessantly invoked by the headsmen, and harpooneers, and bowsmen to do some little job for them; altering, or repairing, or new shaping their various weapons and boat furniture. Often he would be surrounded by an eager circle, all waiting to be served; holding boat-spades, pike-heads, harpoons, and lances, and jealously watching his every sooty movement, as he toiled. Nevertheless, this old man’s was a patient hammer wielded by a patient arm. No murmur, no impatience, no petulance did come from him. Silent, slow, and solemn; bowing over still further his chronically broken back, he toiled away, as if toil were life itself, and the heavy beating of his hammer the heavy beating of his heart. And so it was.—Most miserable!

A peculiar walk in this old man, a certain slight but painful appearing yawing in his gait, had at an early period of the voyage excited the curiosity of the mariners. And to the importunity of their persisted questionings he had finally given in; and so it came to pass that every one now knew the shameful story of his wretched fate.

Belated, and not innocently, one bitter winter’s midnight, on the road running between two country towns, the blacksmith half-stupidly felt the deadly numbness stealing over him, and sought refuge in a leaning, dilapidated barn. The issue was, the loss of the extremities of both feet. Out of this revelation, part by part, at last came out the four acts of the gladness, and the one long, and as yet uncatastrophied fifth act of the grief of his life’s drama.

He was an old man, who, at the age of nearly sixty, had postponedly encountered that thing in sorrow’s technicals called ruin. He had been an artisan of famed excellence, and with plenty to do; owned a house and garden; embraced a youthful, daughter-like, loving wife, and three blithe, ruddy children; every Sunday went to a cheerful-looking church, planted in a grove. But one night, under cover of darkness, and further concealed in a most cunning disguisement, a desperate burglar slid into his happy home, and robbed them all of everything. And darker yet to tell, the blacksmith himself did ignorantly conduct this burglar into his family’s heart. It was the Bottle Conjuror! Upon the opening of that fatal cork, forth flew the fiend, and shrivelled up his home. Now, for prudent, most wise, and economic reasons, the blacksmith’s shop was in the basement of his dwelling, but with a separate entrance to it; so that always had the young and loving healthy wife listened with no unhappy nervousness, but with vigorous pleasure, to the stout ringing of her young-armed old husband’s hammer; whose reverberations, muffled by passing through the floors and walls, came up to her, not unsweetly, in her nursery; and so, to stout Labor’s iron lullaby, the blacksmith’s infants were rocked to slumber.

Oh, woe on woe! Oh, Death, why canst thou not sometimes be timely? Hadst thou taken this old blacksmith to thyself ere his full ruin came upon him, then had the young widow had a delicious grief, and her orphans a truly venerable, legendary sire to dream of in their after years; and all of them a care-killing competency. But Death plucked down some virtuous elder brother, on whose whistling daily toil solely hung the responsibilities of some other family, and left the worse than useless old man standing, till the hideous rot of life should make him easier to harvest.

Why tell the whole? The blows of the basement hammer every day grew more and more between; and each blow every day grew fainter than the last; the wife sat frozen at the window, with tearless eyes, glitteringly gazing into the weeping faces of her children; the bellows fell; the forge choked up with cinders; the house was sold; the mother dived down into the long church-yard grass; her children twice followed her thither; and the houseless, familyless old man staggered off a vagabond in crape; his every woe unreverenced; his grey head a scorn to flaxen curls!

Death seems the only desirable sequel for a career like this; but Death is only a launching into the region of the strange Untried; it is but the first salutation to the possibilities of the immense Remote, the Wild, the Watery, the Unshored; therefore, to the death-longing eyes of such men, who still have left in them some interior compunctions against suicide, does the all-contributed and all-receptive ocean alluringly spread forth his whole plain of unimaginable, taking terrors, and wonderful, new-life adventures; and from the hearts of infinite Pacifics, the thousand mermaids sing to them—“Come hither, broken-hearted; here is another life without the guilt of intermediate death; here are wonders supernatural, without dying for them. Come hither! bury thyself in a life which, to your now equally abhorred and abhorring, landed world, is more oblivious than death. Come hither! put up thy gravestone, too, within the churchyard, and come hither, till we marry thee!”
Hearkening to these voices, East and West, by early sunrise, and by fall of eve, the blacksmith’s soul responded, Aye, I come! And so Perth went a-whaling.

modern_en.title: Chapter 112 — The Blacksmith
paragraphs: Taking advantage of the mild, summer-cool weather that now reigned in these latitudes, and in preparation for the especially active pursuits expected shortly, Perth, the begrimed, blistered old blacksmith, had not moved his portable forge back to the hold after finishing his share of the work on Ahab's leg, but kept it on deck, lashed fast to ringbolts by the foremast; for he was now almost constantly called on by the headsmen, and harpooners, and bowsmen to do some little job for them — altering, or repairing, or reshaping their various weapons and boat gear. Often he would be surrounded by an eager circle, all waiting to be served, holding boat-spades, pike-heads, harpoons and lances, and jealously watching his every sooty movement as he toiled. Nevertheless, this old man's was a patient hammer wielded by a patient arm. No murmur, no impatience, no petulance came from him. Silent, slow and solemn, bowing his chronically broken back still further, he toiled away as if toil were life itself, and the heavy beating of his hammer the heavy beating of his heart. And so it was. — Most miserable!

The old man walked in an odd way, with a slight lurch in his step that looked painful, and early in the voyage this had made the sailors curious. They had kept pestering him with questions until he finally gave in, and so now everyone knew the shameful story of his miserable fate.

Out late, and not innocently, one bitter winter midnight on the road between two country towns, the blacksmith, half-stupefied, felt the deadly numbness stealing over him, and took refuge in a leaning, dilapidated barn. The outcome was the loss of the ends of both his feet. From this revelation, piece by piece, there at last emerged the four acts of gladness, and the one long fifth act of grief, its catastrophe not yet reached, of his life's drama.

He was an old man who, at the age of nearly sixty, had belatedly encountered that thing called, in the technical language of sorrow, ruin. He had been a craftsman of famed excellence, with plenty to do; he owned a house and garden, embraced a youthful, daughter-like, loving wife and three merry, rosy-cheeked children, and every Sunday went to a cheerful-looking church planted in a grove. But one night, under cover of darkness, and further concealed in a most cunning disguise, a desperate burglar slid into his happy home and robbed them all of everything. And darker still to tell, it was the blacksmith himself who unknowingly led this burglar into the heart of his family. It was the Bottle Conjuror! When that fatal cork was drawn, out flew the fiend and shriveled up his home. Now, for prudent, most wise and economical reasons, the blacksmith's shop was in the basement of his house, but with a separate entrance of its own; so the young, loving, healthy wife had always listened — with no unhappy nervousness, but with vigorous pleasure — to the stout ringing of her young-armed old husband's hammer, whose echoes, muffled by passing through the floors and walls, came up to her, not unsweetly, in her nursery; and so, to stout Labor's iron lullaby, the blacksmith's infants were rocked to sleep.

Oh, woe on woe! Oh, Death, why can you not sometimes come in time? Had you taken this old blacksmith to yourself before his full ruin came upon him, then the young widow would have had a delicious grief, and her orphans a truly venerable, legendary father to dream of in their later years; and all of them a care-killing sufficiency to live on. But Death plucked down some virtuous elder brother, on whose whistling daily toil alone hung the responsibilities of some other family, and left the worse-than-useless old man standing, until the hideous rot of life should make him easier to harvest.

Why tell all of it? Every day the blows of the hammer in the basement came farther apart, and every day each blow was fainter than the one before. The wife sat frozen at the window, her eyes tearless and glittering as she stared into the weeping faces of her children. The bellows fell still; the forge clogged with cinders; the house was sold; the mother sank down into the long grass of the churchyard; twice her children followed her there; and the old man, without house or family, staggered off as a tramp in mourning crape, with no one to respect his sorrows, his gray head mocked by flaxen curls!

Death seems the only desirable sequel for a career like this; but Death is only a launching into the region of the strange Untried; it is only the first greeting to the possibilities of the immense Remote, the Wild, the Watery, the Unshored. Therefore, to the death-longing eyes of such men, who still have left in them some inward scruples against suicide, the all-contributed and all-receptive ocean alluringly spreads out his whole plain of unimaginable, captivating terrors and wonderful, new-life adventures; and from the hearts of infinite Pacifics the thousand mermaids sing to them: "Come to us, broken-hearted; here is another life without the guilt of dying in between; here are supernatural wonders, without dying for them. Come to us! Bury yourself in a life which, to your landed world, now equally abhorred and abhorring, is more oblivious than death. Come to us! You too, put up your gravestone within the churchyard, and come to us, till we marry you!"
Listening to these voices, East and West, at early sunrise and at nightfall, the blacksmith's soul answered: Aye, I come! And so Perth went a-whaling.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 112 — Smeden
paragraphs: Det var mildt, sommerkøligt vejr på disse breddegrader, og der ventedes snart især travle jagter. Derfor havde Perth, den sodsværtede, vablede gamle smed, ikke flyttet sin transportable esse tilbage i lasten, da han var færdig med sin del af arbejdet på Ahabs ben, men havde den stående på dækket, surret fast til ringboltene ved formasten; for nu blev han næsten uafbrudt kaldt på af harpunererne og styrmændene og forreste roere, som skulle have lavet et eller andet lille arbejde — ændret, repareret eller omformet deres forskellige våben og bådudstyr. Ofte stod han omringet af en ivrig kreds, der alle ventede på at få deres ting ordnet, med bådspader, spydspidser, harpuner og lanser i hænderne, og de fulgte skinsygt hver eneste af hans sodede bevægelser, mens han slog. Alligevel var denne gamle mands hammer en tålmodig hammer, svunget af en tålmodig arm. Ikke et knurren, ingen utålmodighed, intet gnavent kom fra ham. Tavs, langsom og højtidelig, med sin evigt knækkede ryg bøjet endnu lidt dybere, slog han løs, som om slid var selve livet og hammerens tunge slag hans hjertes tunge slag. Og det var det også. — Mest ulykkelige!

Den gamle mand gik besynderligt, med et lille slingrende ryk i skridtet, som så smerteligt ud, og tidligt på rejsen havde det gjort sømændene nysgerrige. De havde ved med at plage ham med spørgsmål, til han til sidst gav efter, og nu kendte alle den skammelige historie om hans elendige skæbne.

En bitter vinternat ved midnat var smeden ude sent, og ikke i uskyldigt ærinde, på vejen mellem to landsbyer. Halvt bedøvet mærkede han den dødelige følelsesløshed krybe ind over sig og søgte ly i en skæv, faldefærdig lade. Resultatet var, at han mistede enderne af begge fødder. Af denne tilståelse, stykke for stykke, trådte der endelig frem de fire glædens akter og den ene lange femte sorgens akt, hvis katastrofe endnu ikke var nået, i hans livs skuespil.

Han var en gammel mand, som i en alder af næsten tres år sent havde mødt det, der på sorgens fagsprog kaldes ruin. Han havde været en håndværker med berømt dygtighed og masser at lave; han ejede hus og have, havde en ung, datterlignende, kærlig hustru i sine arme og tre glade, rosenkindede børn, og hver søndag gik han i en kirke med et muntert udseende, der lå i en lund. Men en nat, i dække af mørket og yderligere skjult i en yderst snedig forklædning, smuttede en desperat indbrudstyv ind i hans lykkelige hjem og røvede dem alle for alt. Og endnu mørkere at fortælle: det var smeden selv, der uvidende havde ført denne tyv ind i hjertet af sin familie. Det var Flaskebesværgeren! Da den skæbnesvangre prop blev trukket, fløj fanden ud og skrumpede hans hjem ind. Nu lå smedens værksted af kloge, vise og sparsommelige grunde i kælderen under hans hus, men med sin egen separate indgang; så den unge, kærlige, raske hustru havde altid lyttet — uden ulykkelig nervøsitet, men med kraftfuld glæde — til sin gamle mands kraftige hammerslag fra de unge arme, hvis ekko, dæmpet på vej gennem gulve og vægge, nåede hende, ikke uskønt, i børneværelset; og således blev smedens små vugget i søvn til det kraftfulde arbejdes jernvuggevise.

Å, ve over ve! Å, død, hvorfor kan du ikke nogle gange komme i tide? Havde du taget denne gamle smed til dig, før hans fulde ruin ramte ham, så ville den unge enke have haft en dejlig sorg og hendes forældreløse en virkelig ærværdig, legendarisk far at drømme om i deres senere år, og dem alle sammen et sorgfrit udkomme. Men døden plukkede en dydig ældre bror, på hvis fløjtende daglige slid alene en anden families ansvar hvilede, og lod den værre end ubrugelige gamle mand stå, til livets afskyelige råd kunne gøre ham lettere at høste.

Hvorfor fortælle det hele? Dag for dag kom hammerslagene i kælderen med længere mellemrum, og dag for dag var hvert slag svagere end det foregående. Hustruen sad stivnet ved vinduet med tåreløse, glitrende øjne og stirrede ind i sine børns grædende ansigter. Bælgen sank i tavshed; essen tilstoppedes af slagger; huset blev solgt; moderen sank ned i kirkegårdens lange græs; to gange fulgte hendes børn efter; og den gamle mand vaklede uden hus og familie af sted som en landstryger i sørgeflor, uden at nogen respekterede hans sorg, og hans grå hoved hånet af blonde krøller!

Døden synes den eneste ønskværdige fortsættelse på et liv som dette; men døden er kun en søsætning ud i det underlige Uprøvedes rige; den er kun første hilsen til mulighederne i det umådelige Fjerne, det Vilde, det Vandige, det Kystløse. Derfor udbreder det alt-bidragende og alt-modtagende hav lokkende hele sin slette af ufattelige, fængslende rædsler og vidunderlige eventyr i nyt liv for øjnene af sådanne mænd, som længes efter døden, men som stadig har noget indre betænkelighed ved selvmord; og fra uendelige Stillehavs hjerter synger de tusind havfruer til dem: »Kom til os, I knuste hjerter; her er et andet liv uden skylden ved at dø imellem; her er overnaturlige undere, uden at I skal dø for dem. Kom til os! Begrav jer i et liv, som for jeres landverden, der nu er lige afskyet og afskyende, er mere glemt end døden. Kom til os! I skal også sætte jeres gravsten op på kirkegården og komme til os, til vi gifter jer!«
Mens han lyttede til disse stemmer, øst og vest, ved tidlig solopgang og ved aftenens frembrud, svarede smedens sjæl: Ja, jeg kommer! Og så tog Perth på hvalfangst.
